text: Rules mod m; digit sums mod 9; division blocks.

Working modulo m (模意义下) keeps numbers small: replace every intermediate result by its remainder. Addition, subtraction and multiplication can be reduced at any moment; division cannot (that needs an inverse, 19.2).

a ≡ b (mod m) means m divides a − b. In C++ the % of a negative number is negative, so write (a - b) % m + m) % m when a − b may be below 0. A product of two numbers below 10⁹ fits in long long; below 10¹⁸ it needs __int128 .

lines: Rule Formula Note
add (a + b) mod m = ((a mod m) + (b mod m)) mod m reduce first, then add
subtract (a − b) mod m = ((a mod m) − (b mod m) + m) mod m add m to stay ≥ 0
multiply (a·b) mod m = ((a mod m)·(b mod m)) mod m watch the product size
power aᵇ mod m by repeated squaring O(log b), 第3章
divide a / b mod m = a · b⁻¹ mod m only if gcd(b, m) = 1

text: Every power of 10 is ≡ 1 (mod 9), so a number is ≡ its digit sum, and gluing numbers together is ≡ adding them (P4942). The sum l + … + r has a formula; with l, r up to 10¹² the product (l + r)(r − l + 1) would overflow, so halve the even factor first and reduce each factor mod 9.
Halving is a division: do it on the exact value, before taking the remainder. Afterwards only +, −, × are safe.

Σi=1..n (k mod i) (P2261): rewrite k mod i = k − i·⌊k/i⌋. The value ⌊k/i⌋ takes only about 2√k different values, and the i with the same value form a block [l, r] with r = ⌊k / ⌊k/l⌋⌋. Add each block at once: division blocks (整除分块), O(√k).
For i > k the quotient is 0, so the loop stops at min(n, k). The same blocks appear in P2568, P6583 and any sum with ⌊n/i⌋ inside.
Fermat, extended Euclid, the linear table.

The inverse (乘法逆元) of a modulo m is x with a·x ≡ 1 (mod m), written a⁻¹. It exists exactly when gcd(a, m) = 1. Then "divide by a" means "multiply by a⁻¹", so fractions like p / q mod m make sense (P2613).

Method How When Fermat a⁻¹ = ap−2 mod p p prime, one inverse, O(log p) extended Euclid solve a·x + m·y = 1 any m with gcd(a, m) = 1, O(log m) linear table inv[i] = −⌊p/i⌋ · inv[p mod i] mod p all of 1 … n, p prime, O(n) factorial trick inv(n!) by Fermat, then inv(i!) = inv((i+1)!) · (i+1) binomials, O(n + log p)
Why the table works: write p = q·i + r with q = ⌊p/i⌋, r = p mod i. Then q·i + r ≡ 0, so i ≡ −r / q, and i⁻¹ ≡ −q · r⁻¹ (mod p). Since r < i, inv[r] is already known (P3811).
Check one: 2 × 7 = 14 ≡ 1 (mod 13), so inv[2] = 7. Writing (p − p / i) instead of −(p / i) keeps everything non-negative.
Fermat needs p prime and a not divisible by p. For a composite modulus use extended Euclid, and first check that gcd(a, m) = 1.

title: 同余方程与中国剩余定理

text: exgcd, Bézout, congruences, CRT.

Extended Euclid (扩展欧几里得): besides g = gcd(a, b) it finds x, y with a·x + b·y = g. From gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b): if b·x′ + (a mod b)·y′ = g, then x = y′ and y = x′ − ⌊a/b⌋·y′. Bézout: a·x + b·y = c has integer solutions exactly when g divides c (P4549).
Linear congruence a·x ≡ c (mod m) is a·x + m·y = c. Solve a·x₀ + m·y₀ = g, require g | c, then x = x₀·(c / g); all solutions differ by m / g, so the smallest non-negative one is x mod (m / g).
Impossible

The frogs (P1516) meet after t jumps when x + m·t ≡ y + n·t (mod L): a linear congruence in t. Make the coefficient positive first; reduce t and c / g modulo L / g before multiplying. P1082 is the same with c = 1 and g = 1 guaranteed.

CRT (中国剩余定理): x ≡ ri (mod mi) with pairwise coprime mi has exactly one solution modulo M = Π mi. Build it from pieces: Mi·(Mi⁻¹ mod mi) is 1 mod mi and 0 mod every other modulus; multiply by ri and add (P1495).

16 = 1 mod 3, 1 mod 5, 2 mod 7. Products reach M ≈ 10¹⁸, so multiply in __int128. If the moduli are not coprime, merge the equations two at a time with extended Euclid (excrt); 荒岛野人(P2421) tries each answer and checks pairs with a congruence.
That one static_cast<long long>(ans) is needed: cout cannot print __int128 directly, and ans < M fits in long long.

title: 线性筛与积性函数(选读)

text: Each composite crossed once; φ and μ on the way.
green: primes; others crossed once each

The linear sieve (线性筛 , 欧拉筛) finds all primes up to n in O(n): for each i, cross out i·p for primes p ≤ (smallest prime factor of i). Then every composite is crossed exactly once, by its smallest prime factor, unlike the Eratosthenes sieve.
The rule "stop when p divides i" is what makes it linear: if p | i then i·p′ for a larger prime p′ has smallest prime p, so it will be crossed later from a different i.

A function is multiplicative (积性函数) if f(ab) = f(a)·f(b) whenever gcd(a, b) = 1: Euler φ, the Möbius μ, the number of divisors d. The sieve computes them for free, because it meets each n as i·p and knows whether p already divides i.
Case in the sieve φ μ i is a new prime φ(i) = i − 1 μ(i) = −1 p does not divide i φ(i·p) = φ(i)·(p − 1) μ(i·p) = −μ(i) p divides i φ(i·p) = φ(i)·p μ(i·p) = 0
Guard of honour (P2158): standing at a corner of an n × n grid, you see (x, y) exactly when gcd(x, y) = 1. Counting coprime pairs row by row gives φ, so the answer is 3 + 2·Σi=2..n−1 φ(i).
The break when p | i is the whole trick: both the linear time and the "p divides i" formula depend on it.
φ(n), gcd sums, the extended Euler theorem.

Euler's function φ(n) (欧拉函数) counts 1 ≤ k ≤ n with gcd(k, n) = 1. From the factorisation n = Π pe: φ(n) = n · Π (1 − 1/p). One value costs O(√n) by trial division; many values come from the sieve (19.4).

Euler's theorem: if gcd(a, m) = 1 then aφ(m) ≡ 1 (mod m); for prime m this is Fermat. Extended version (扩展欧拉定理) for any a: if b ≥ φ(m), then ab ≡ a(b mod φ(m)) + φ(m) (mod m). It shrinks huge exponents (P5091, P4139).
Σi=1..n gcd(i, n) (P2303): group i by d = gcd(i, n). gcd(i, n) = d ⇔ i = d·k with gcd(k, n/d) = 1, so there are φ(n/d) of them. Answer = Σd | n d·φ(n/d).
For n = 6: 1·φ(6) + 2·φ(3) + 3·φ(2) + 6·φ(1) = 2 + 4 + 3 + 6 = 15. Grouping by the gcd is the standard first step for every gcd sum (P2568 counts prime gcds the same way).

Read the exponent as a string, reduce it mod φ(m) digit by digit, and remember whether it ever reached φ(m). Only then add φ(m) back: for small b the plain exponent must be used, because the extended rule needs b ≥ φ(m).
210²¹ mod 10: φ(10) = 4, 10²¹ mod 4 = 0, so the exponent becomes 4 and 2⁴ = 16 ≡ 6. Here gcd(2, 10) = 2, and plain Euler would wrongly give 2⁰ = 1.
The Luogu problems for this chapter, a ladder through them, and experiments to try yourself.
Key points to memorise
1. +, −, × can be reduced anytime; ÷ needs an inverse; (a − b) % m + m.
2. Division blocks: r = k / (k / l); about 2√k blocks.
3. Inverse: Fermat a^(p−2); exgcd for any coprime m; table inv[i] = (p − p/i)·inv[p % i] % p.
4. exgcd: x = y′, y = x′ − (a/b)·y′; a·x + b·y = c solvable ⇔ gcd | c.
5. a·x ≡ c (mod m): x = x₀·(c/g) mod (m/g).
6. CRT: Σ rᵢ·Mᵢ·(Mᵢ⁻¹ mod mᵢ) mod M; __int128 for the products.
7. Linear sieve: break when p | i; φ(ip) = φ(i)·p or φ(i)·(p − 1).
8. φ(n) = n·Π(1 − 1/p); Σ gcd(i, n) = Σ_{d|n} d·φ(n/d).
9. b ≥ φ(m): aᵇ ≡ a^(b mod φ(m) + φ(m)) (mod m), for any a.
